name: Tokyo
tagline: The world's largest metropolitan area, a genuine collection of distinct neighbourhoods rather than one city, running from neon-lit crossings to quiet shrine precincts within a few train stops of each other.
highlight: Shibuya Crossing at rush hour, thousands of people crossing from every direction at once in a scene that somehow stays completely orderly.
shortDescription: Japan's capital, a vast collection of distinct neighbourhoods spanning ultra-modern technology, deep tradition and one of the world's great food cities.
metaDescription: A Tokyo travel guide: Shibuya, Asakusa, Shinjuku, the best neighbourhoods, when to go and a practical four-day itinerary.
knownFor: Shibuya Crossing, Asakusa's temples, world-class food

image.file: File:Neon in the streets of Shibuya (9412153000).jpg
image.alt: Tokyo's Shibuya streets at night, illuminated by neon signage

intro: Tokyo is less a single city than a federation of neighbourhoods, each with a distinct character and, in many cases, its own historic identity as a separate town absorbed into the wider metropolis over centuries. Shibuya's youth culture, Asakusa's old-town temples, Ginza's luxury shopping and Akihabara's electronics-and-anime density all sit within the same city while feeling like entirely different places.

The scale is difficult to grasp before arriving — greater Tokyo holds well over 35 million people, making it the largest metropolitan area on earth, yet the city's train network and clear neighbourhood boundaries make it feel navigable rather than overwhelming once the initial orientation passes.

What consistently surprises first-time visitors is how completely the city's reputation for cutting-edge technology coexists with genuine, working tradition — a centuries-old shrine sits a short walk from a robot-staffed café, and both are treated with equally serious attention by the people who use them daily.

whyVisit.intro: Tokyo's case is that no other city fits this much genuine variety, this reliably well organised, into one metropolitan area.

points.title: The neighbourhood variety is vast
points.text: Few cities anywhere shift character this completely between adjacent districts, each with its own real identity rather than a single downtown core.

points.title: The food scene is world class
points.text: From convenience store meals to Michelin-starred restaurants, Tokyo's food culture holds a serious standard at every single price point.

points.title: The public transport is excellent
points.text: Dense, punctual and precisely signed rail and subway networks make a city this large feel manageable within days of arrival.

points.title: It's safe, at any hour
points.text: Among the safest major cities in the world, allowing exploration late into the night without the caution larger cities usually demand.

points.title: It works as both a destination and a gateway
points.text: A complete trip on its own, and the natural starting point for the rest of the country by shinkansen.

attractionsIntro: Tokyo's essential sights, spanning its old-town temples, its neon-lit crossings and its quieter imperial grounds.

attractions.name: Senso-ji Temple, Asakusa

image.alt: Senso-ji Temple, Tokyo's oldest and most significant Buddhist temple

attractions.text: Tokyo's oldest and most significant Buddhist temple, its approach lined by the Nakamise shopping street's traditional snacks and souvenirs, busy but worthwhile.
attractions.tip: Arrive before 9am to see the temple grounds before the day's crowds and tour groups build up.

attractions.name: Shibuya Crossing

image.alt: Crowds crossing at Shibuya Scramble Crossing

attractions.text: The world's busiest pedestrian crossing, thousands of people moving through from every direction at once, a mesmerising piece of organised urban chaos.
attractions.tip: The Shibuya Sky observation deck or a window seat at the Starbucks overlooking the crossing both offer a good elevated view.

attractions.name: Meiji Shrine

image.alt: The great torii gate at the entrance to Meiji Shrine

attractions.text: A serene Shinto shrine set within genuine forest in the heart of the city, dedicated to Emperor Meiji, offering a real contrast to Harajuku's busy streets just outside its gates.
attractions.tip: Walk in via the main Omotesando approach through the torii gate for the full, unhurried effect.

attractions.name: Tokyo Skytree

image.alt: Tokyo Skytree rising above the city in spring

attractions.text: One of the world's tallest towers, its observation decks offering sweeping views across the entire metropolitan area on a clear day.
attractions.tip: Book timed-entry tickets online ahead to skip a queue that can otherwise run to an hour or more.

attractions.name: teamLab digital art museum

image.alt: An immersive light installation inside teamLab Borderless in Tokyo

attractions.text: An immersive digital art experience across vast, disorienting rooms of light and projection, among the most distinctive museum experiences anywhere.
attractions.tip: Wear light, plain clothing — some rooms reflect and project onto visitors, and busy patterns compete with the artwork.

attractions.name: The Imperial Palace East Gardens

image.alt: Landscaped grounds of the Imperial Palace East Gardens in Tokyo

attractions.text: Part of the working Imperial Palace grounds, peaceful landscaped gardens open to the public free of charge in the heart of the city.
attractions.tip: The gardens close on Mondays and Fridays — check the current schedule before planning a visit.

thingsToDoIntro: Beyond the major sights, Tokyo rewards its neighbourhood contrasts and its serious food culture.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Shinjuku's Golden Gai and nightlife

image.alt: The narrow, neon-lit alleyways of Shinjuku's Golden Gai at night

thingsToDo.text: A tiny warren of alleyways packed with minuscule bars, each seating only a handful of people, an atmospheric slice of old Tokyo nightlife.
thingsToDo.tip: Some Golden Gai bars charge a cover fee and are locals-only in practice — look for English signage welcoming visitors before entering.

thingsToDo.title: Ride the trains like a local

image.file: File:JRE E235 Yamanote Line 04 set Tokyo Station 2017-07-09 (35765917051).jpg
image.alt: A Yamanote line train at Tokyo Station

thingsToDo.text: Tokyo's rail network is one of the best in the world, and simply riding it between neighbourhoods is part of experiencing the city properly.
thingsToDo.tip: Get a Suica or Pasmo IC card immediately on arrival — it covers nearly all transport and many small purchases on one card.

thingsToDo.title: Eat at a standing ramen counter

image.file: File:Ramen Cooking Tokyo - ramen sushi sake set.jpg
image.alt: A ramen counter meal in Tokyo

thingsToDo.text: Some of the city's best ramen comes from small, unpretentious counters ordered by ticket machine, eaten quickly among locals rather than lingered over.
thingsToDo.tip: A queue of locals outside a tiny counter is a far more reliable sign of quality than any online review.

thingsToDo.title: Wander Akihabara's electronics and anime streets
thingsToDo.text: Tokyo's dedicated electronics and otaku culture district, dense with multi-storey shops, arcades and anime and manga specialists.
thingsToDo.tip: Duty-free electronics shops require your passport at purchase — carry it if planning to buy anything significant.

thingsToDo.title: Try a themed café or a genuine karaoke session

image.alt: A cat café in Tokyo's Yanaka district

thingsToDo.text: From cat and owl cafés to private karaoke boxes rented by the hour, Tokyo's leisure culture runs to distinctive, easy-to-join experiences.
thingsToDo.tip: Private karaoke rooms are rented by the hour and welcoming to non-Japanese speakers — song lists include an English-language menu.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Toyosu Market's tuna auction and sushi breakfast
thingsToDo.text: Tokyo's relocated fish market still runs a serious early-morning tuna auction, with excellent sushi breakfast counters nearby for those awake early enough.
thingsToDo.tip: The tuna auction viewing requires an early, sometimes pre-booked start — check current access rules before planning around it.

foodIntro: Tokyo's food scene spans every price point with a consistent standard, from standing counters to some of the world's most acclaimed restaurants.

foods.name: Edomae sushi
foods.text: Tokyo's own historic sushi style, developed in the city under its old name of Edo, typically served without excess garnish to let the fish itself lead.
foods.whereToTry: Counters throughout the Ginza and Toyosu areas, from affordable conveyor-belt chains to high-end omakase.

foods.name: Tokyo-style shoyu ramen

image.alt: A bowl of Tokyo-style shoyu ramen

foods.text: A soy-sauce-based broth, generally lighter than Kyushu's tonkotsu style, Tokyo's own defining regional ramen variation.
foods.whereToTry: Standing ramen counters citywide, with a queue of locals a reliable sign of quality.

foods.name: Tempura

image.alt: A plate of freshly fried tempura

foods.text: Lightly battered, deep-fried seafood and vegetables, done at its best with fresh oil and split-second timing at a dedicated counter.
foods.whereToTry: Dedicated tempura counter restaurants, particularly around Ginza and Asakusa.

foods.name: Monjayaki

image.file: File:Monjayaki dish from Tsukishima, Tokyo, Japan; January 2013.jpg
image.alt: Monjayaki cooking on a griddle in Tsukishima, Tokyo

foods.text: A runny, savoury batter dish cooked directly at the table, a genuine Tokyo speciality distinct from Osaka's firmer okonomiyaki.
foods.whereToTry: Tsukishima's 'Monja Street', the dish's genuine spiritual home in the city.

foods.name: Yakitori
foods.text: Skewered, grilled chicken parts, eaten at small smoky counters that are a genuine after-work Tokyo institution.
foods.whereToTry: The yakitori alleys around Yurakucho and Omoide Yokocho near Shinjuku station.

foods.name: Convenience store food

image.alt: Bento and onigiri rice balls from a Lawson convenience store

foods.text: Tokyo's konbini culture is excellent, not a last resort — onigiri, sandwiches and hot food from 7-Eleven, Lawson or FamilyMart hold up as legitimately good meals.
foods.whereToTry: Any convenience store citywide, open 24 hours and reliable at any budget.

accommodation.intro: Tokyo's size means the right neighbourhood matters more than in most cities — pick a base near your priorities.

areas.name: Shinjuku
areas.text: A major transport hub with excellent connections citywide, alongside some of Tokyo's best nightlife and dining density.

areas.name: Asakusa
areas.text: A more traditional, lower-key base near Senso-ji, generally offering better value than the central districts.

areas.name: Shibuya
areas.text: Tokyo's most iconic modern district, putting the crossing, shopping and nightlife directly on your doorstep.

gettingThere.intro: Tokyo is served by two major airports, with excellent rail connections into the city centre from both.

options.text: The Narita Express and Skyliner both reach central Tokyo in under an hour, the more common arrival point for long-haul international flights.
options.detail: Airport limousine buses offer a slower but direct alternative to hotel-area drop-offs without a transfer.

options.text: Closer to the city centre, reachable by monorail or train in around 30 minutes, increasingly used by international carriers.
options.detail: Generally the more convenient airport if your route offers a choice between the two.

options.text: Bullet trains connect Tokyo to [[kyoto|Kyoto]] in about 2h15 and to [[osaka-nara|Osaka]] in around 2h30.
options.detail: Book reserved seats a day or two ahead in peak season, including cherry blossom time.

gettingAround.intro: Tokyo's rail and subway network is dense, punctual and easy to navigate once the initial system makes sense.

options.text: A combination of JR lines, Tokyo Metro and Toei Subway covers the entire city, all usable on a single Suica or Pasmo IC card.
options.detail: Google Maps handles Tokyo's transit routing reliably, including platform and exit numbers.

options.text: Individual neighbourhoods are walkable once you arrive, with most major sights within a district clustered close together.
options.detail: Station exits can surface several blocks from where you expect — check the exit number before climbing the stairs.

options.text: Reliable and clean, though considerably more expensive than rail for any distance a train also covers.
options.detail: Doors open and close automatically — do not touch them yourself.

bestTime.headline: March–May and October–November, for cherry blossoms or clear autumn skies
bestTime.summary: Tokyo's climate is humid in summer, and spring and autumn offer the most comfortable balance of weather and the city's best natural moments.

seasons.text: Cherry blossoms in late March into April draw real crowds for good reason, with comfortable temperatures across the season.
Hot, humid and prone to a June rainy season, though also lively with summer festivals across the city.
Comfortable temperatures and clear skies, with spectacular foliage in the city's larger parks by November.
Cold but usually clear and dry, with illuminations and a festive citywide atmosphere through December.

bestTime.avoid: Golden Week (late April into early May) without accommodation booked well ahead, when domestic travel surges nationwide.

itinerary.title: Four days in Tokyo
itinerary.intro: Central sights first, then the city's contrasting neighbourhoods at an unhurried pace.

days.title: Asakusa and central Tokyo
days.summary: Old Tokyo and the Imperial Palace.
days.morning: Senso-ji Temple and the Nakamise shopping street.
days.evening: Dinner in Ueno or back toward Asakusa.

days.title: Shibuya and Harajuku
days.morning: Meiji Shrine and Harajuku's Takeshita Street.

days.title: Shinjuku and a digital art museum
days.morning: teamLab or another digital art experience.
days.evening: Omoide Yokocho's yakitori alleys and Golden Gai.

days.title: Akihabara and Tokyo Skytree
days.evening: A final dinner of your choice — Tokyo rewards returning to a favourite from earlier in the trip.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on transport, timing and etiquette that make a real difference to a Tokyo trip.
tips: Get a Suica or Pasmo IC card immediately on arrival — it covers nearly all transport and many small purchases.
Book teamLab and other popular timed-entry attractions online well ahead, especially in peak season.
Carry cash — many smaller restaurants and shops remain cash-only despite the city's high-tech reputation.
Keep phone calls off trains — step between cars if a call is unavoidable.
Check station exit numbers before climbing the stairs — Tokyo's larger stations surface several blocks apart.
Book cherry blossom season accommodation many months ahead if visiting in late March or April.
Try at least one standing ramen counter and one convenience store meal — both are representative of the city's food culture, not just budget options.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Tokyo?
faq.a: Four to five for a first visit. Three covers the essential sights at a rushed pace; five allows proper time for individual neighbourhoods and a day trip to Nikko or Hakone.

faq.q: Do I need to speak Japanese in Tokyo?
faq.a: No — English signage is common on transport and in tourist areas, and a translation app covers most other situations, though spoken English is limited away from tourist-facing businesses.
Less than its reputation suggests. Mid-range travel runs about ¥15,000–28,000 per person per day, and excellent, cheap meals are easy to find at convenience stores and standing counters.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.a: March to May and October to November offer the best weather — cherry blossoms in spring, clear skies and foliage in autumn. Summer is hot and humid; winter is cold but clear.
Exceptionally so, among the safest major cities in the world, with very low rates of violent crime and theft even late at night in busy districts.
